title: Twenty-minute deep dive: marathon training
description: Priya and Sam spend about twenty minutes on Sam's first marathon, moving through the training plan, shoes and gear, an old IT-band injury, fuelling, the mental side, race-day strategy and life balance, each with several distinct sub-questions. Expect 12–30 nodes, with long subtopics split into specific level-2 ideas and no level-1 node longer than 5 minutes without children.

utterances.text: So, four months. How are you actually feeling about it now that the registration's paid and there's no backing out?

Honestly? Half excited, half terrified. I downloaded a plan last week and I've been staring at it like it's a tax form. It's one of those sixteen week beginner ones. Four runs a week, and one long run on Sunday that creeps up until you hit twenty miles about three weeks before the race.
Twenty is the peak? Not the full twenty six?
Yeah, that's what threw me. The plan says you never run the full distance in training, which feels like cheating. How am I supposed to know I can do it if I've never done it?

No, that's totally normal. Nobody I know ran the full thing beforehand. The adrenaline and the taper basically cover the last six miles. If you run twenty six in training you just spend two weeks recovering from it.
What's your long run at right now?
Ten miles last Sunday. It took me just under an hour forty and I felt fine until about mile eight, then my legs got really heavy.
That's a good base though. Ten miles four months out is honestly more than most first timers have.

Right, but here's my question. The plan jumps from ten to twelve in two weeks, and my friend Marco says I should be following the ten percent rule, which would mean eleven, then twelve point one or whatever.

Ugh, the ten percent rule. It's fine as a rough guide, but it's about weekly mileage, not one run. If your whole week goes from twenty five miles to twenty seven, that's well under ten percent even if the long run grows by two. And most plans build in a cutback week every third or fourth week too.
Oh, so the lower weeks are on purpose. I thought that was a typo.
No, that's the plan letting your body catch up. Don't skip them and don't sneak extra miles in.

Okay. And the other thing I genuinely don't get is the pace stuff. The plan says most runs should be easy, conversational pace, and then there's one day of intervals. But when I run slow it feels like I'm not training at all.
That's the trap everyone falls into. You go out, you run every single run at the same medium hard pace, and you end up tired all the time and not actually any faster.
Easy should be properly easy. Like, you could talk to me the whole time. For you that's probably more than a minute per mile slower than what you'd race at.
A minute slower? That feels embarrassing. People walking their dogs are going to pass me.

Let them. The easy miles build the engine, all the aerobic stuff. Then the Tuesday intervals are where you actually get to feel fast. Eight times four hundred metres, or mile repeats, whatever the plan says.
Yeah, it's mile repeats. Three of them, building up to six.
Those will hurt. In a good way. Mostly.
Speaking of hurting, I need to ask you about shoes, because the guy at the running shop tried to sell me a two hundred and fifty dollar pair with a carbon plate.
Oh no. Which ones?
Some super bouncy racing shoe. He said they'd make me four percent faster.
I mean, that number comes from elite runners in a lab. For you, right now, they're mostly going to make your calves sore.
Really? Not faster at all?

They might help a bit on race day. But the plate is stiff and the foam is soft and kind of unstable, and if you train in them every day your feet and lower legs don't do as much work. A lot of people save them for the race and a couple of long runs to practise.
So I'd be paying two fifty for one day.
Basically. If you want them, buy them in the last month and wear them for two long runs so they're broken in. Not before.
What are you running in now?
The same pair I've had for, like, a year and a half. They're kind of grey now. They used to be blue.
Sam.
I know, I know.

Most shoes are done somewhere around three to five hundred miles. And honestly, what a lot of people do is rotate two pairs. One cushioned daily trainer, and one a little lighter for the faster days. The foam gets a day to recover and your legs get slightly different loads.
Is that real, or is that just something shoe companies say so you buy two?
Bit of both, honestly. There's some research linking rotation to fewer injuries, but it's not huge. The main thing is not running four months on dead foam.
Fair. Two pairs then. Oh, and socks, because I have to tell you about the blister.
Oh no, what blister?

So on the ten mile run last Sunday, I wore these cheap cotton socks because everything else was in the wash. By mile six there was this hot spot on the side of my big toe, and I just kept going because I'm an idiot.
Please tell me it didn't pop mid run.
It popped mid run. I got home and the inside of the sock was pink. My partner thought I'd been stabbed.
Oh my god. Okay, cotton is the enemy. You want proper running socks, synthetic or merino, and some people put a bit of anti chafe balm on the spots that rub.
I bought three pairs of the fancy socks the next day. Fourteen dollars each. For socks.
Best fourteen dollars you'll ever spend. Way cheaper than missing a week because you can't get a shoe on.
Has the knee been okay with all this? I remember you limping around at my birthday.
Mostly. That was the IT band thing from two summers ago. It flares up if I do a lot of downhill. It's this sharp pain on the outside of the knee, usually around mile five or six.
Did you ever actually see someone about it, or did you just stop running until it went away?
The second one. Which I know is the wrong answer.
It's the very common answer. But with marathon mileage it's going to come back. Seriously, see a physio before your long runs get past fourteen.
What do they even do? I feel like they'll just tell me to stretch.

Mine did a whole assessment. Watched me run on a treadmill, made me do single leg squats, and found out my hip on that side was super weak, so my knee was caving in every step. The IT band was just where it hurt, not where the problem was.
Huh. So the knee is kind of the victim.
Exactly. The knee is the victim, the hip is the criminal.
Okay, I like that.
Which is why the strength stuff matters so much. Are you doing any?
I do push ups sometimes? Does that count?

For your legs, no. You want things like clamshells, side planks, single leg deadlifts, step downs off a stair, and some proper squats. Two sessions a week, maybe twenty five minutes each. It's boring, but it's the thing that keeps people from getting hurt in month three.
Twenty five minutes twice a week on top of four runs. When am I meant to work?
You can do it straight after an easy run. Or in the living room with a resistance band while something's on TV.
Okay, that's doable. The part I'm worst at is knowing when to stop. Like, if it twinges at mile four of a long run, am I supposed to just bail?

My rule is, if the pain changes how you run, you stop. If you're limping, or you're landing differently to protect it, you walk home or call someone. A dull ache that stays the same is usually fine. A sharp pain that keeps getting worse isn't.
And then what, take a week off?

Usually a couple of days of easy cross training, the bike or the pool, and then a short test run. Missing three days is nothing. Missing six weeks because you pushed through is the thing that actually ruins a marathon.
Okay, can we talk about food? Because on the ten miler I didn't eat anything, and I think that's why mile eight felt like wading through cement.
Yeah, probably. Ten is about where you start running low, especially if you skipped breakfast.
I had a coffee.
A coffee is not breakfast, Sam.
For runs over about ninety minutes you want to take something in. Most people use gels, roughly one every forty five minutes, starting early, not when you're already falling apart.
I tried a gel once. It was like eating warm toothpaste.

They're gross, I'm not going to lie. But there are chews, thinner ones, even dates. The important bit is practising on long runs so your stomach learns to handle it. You don't want to find out at mile fifteen of the race that a gel sends you sprinting for a portable toilet.
Oh god, that's my nightmare.
Which is why you never try anything new on race day. Not a gel, not a breakfast, not socks.
Especially not socks. What about carb loading? Is that just an excuse to eat three plates of pasta?

Kind of, but people do it wrong. It's not one giant dinner the night before. It's the two or three days before, where you shift most of what you eat toward carbs. Rice, bread, potatoes, bagels. And you're running less because you're tapering, so your muscles actually store it.
So the night before should be normal?
A normal sized, boring, carby dinner. Nothing spicy, nothing super high fibre. The worst thing is going somewhere fancy and getting a massive salad and a curry.
There goes my plan for the night before. And water, how much should I be drinking? I've heard people say drink loads and other people say that's dangerous.

Both are sort of right. Drink to thirst mostly, and on long runs carry a bottle or plan a loop past a fountain. On hot days you need electrolytes too, not just water. Overdrinking plain water is actually how people get into real trouble.
That might explain the cramp thing.
What cramp thing?

So in the spring I did that half marathon in the heat, and around mile eleven both calves just locked. Completely. I was hopping on the side of the road, and some guy in a banana costume stopped to help me.
The banana guy saved you?
The banana guy saved me. He gave me salt tablets. I'd been drinking water at every single station and nothing else.

Yeah, that sounds like you were low on sodium, and probably also running harder than your fitness was ready for. Cramping is still a bit of a mystery, but salt and electrolytes definitely help some people. Practise with an electrolyte drink on your hot long runs.
And buy the banana guy a drink if I ever see him again.
Can I ask how you're doing in your head on the long ones? Because ten miles alone is a long time to be with your thoughts.
Honestly, that's the part I didn't expect. The legs are hard, but the boredom is worse. Around the hour mark I start doing maths about how much is left and it just gets depressing.
Oh, the maths spiral. Everyone does it. I'm at six point two, that's sixty percent, no wait...
Exactly that! And then I check my watch every three hundred metres.

One thing that helped me was splitting the run into chunks that aren't distance. The first part is the warm up and I don't care about pace, then it's the river section, then it's the hill, then it's home. You're running to landmarks, not numbers.
I like that. What do you listen to?
Podcasts for easy runs, music for anything hard. Long rambly podcasts are great because you stop noticing the miles. But for intervals I want something loud.
I've been doing music the whole time and I think I've burned out my playlist. I hear the first two notes of certain songs now and I feel tired.
Also, is it true some races ban headphones?

Some do, or they discourage them, mostly for safety. Check yours. And honestly, try a few long runs with nothing at all. It's weird at first, but you get way more in tune with your breathing and your effort, which is exactly what you need on race day.
Okay, I'll try one silent one. Do you have a mantra? Marco keeps saying I need a mantra and I feel silly.

I do, and it's very cheesy. Relax, light, tall. That's it. When I start getting tense, I say it in my head and I drop my shoulders, I try to land quieter, and I stand up straighter. It's less about inspiration and more like a checklist.
That's actually practical. I thought you were going to say something like pain is weakness leaving the body.
No, that one just makes me want to stop.
Here's my real fear though. The wall. Everyone talks about hitting the wall at mile twenty like it's this monster waiting for you.

It's real, but a lot of it is fuel and pacing. If you go out too fast and don't eat, you're basically guaranteed to hit it. If you've practised your gels and you start slow, it usually turns into this is really hard, rather than my body has shut down.
So the wall is kind of self inflicted.
A lot of the time, yes. And it helps to expect the last six miles to be miserable. If you plan for it to be hard, it's way less scary when it actually is.
So how do I not go out too fast? Because I know myself. The gun goes and I'm going to sprint like I'm in a movie.
Everyone does that. Pick a realistic goal pace from your training, and for the first three miles deliberately run slower than it. Like ten to fifteen seconds per mile slower. It'll feel ridiculous.
What's realistic for me? I was vaguely thinking four hours.

Off a ten mile run in an hour forty, four hours is a decent target if training goes well. But I'd have a few goals. A dream goal, a happy goal, and a just finish goal. Then if the day goes badly, you haven't failed, you've just switched goals.
I like that, three goals. What's a negative split? People keep saying it like I should know.

It means you run the second half faster than the first. It's what most good races look like. You hold back, you feel fresh at halfway, and then you're passing people in the last ten kilometres instead of being passed.
Passing people sounds amazing.
Way better than the alternative, where you're at mile twenty two and a woman pushing a stroller goes past you.
That's oddly specific.
It happened in my first one. The stroller was very fast.
Okay, the start itself stresses me out too. They put you in these corrals and there's like thirty thousand people.

Yeah, get in the right corral for your estimated time and don't move up because you're excited. If you start with faster people you get swept along at their pace. Get there early, use the toilets twice, and wear an old jumper you can throw away at the start. They donate them.
The other thing is the first mile will be slow because of the crowd. Don't weave around everyone trying to make up time. That burns so much energy.
And then mile twenty. What do I actually do at mile twenty?

Mile twenty is where the race really starts, that's the cliché. Practically, take your gel, check in with your mantra, and think about one mile at a time. Don't think about six point two. Just get to the next water station, then the next one.
One mile at a time. Not maths.
Not maths. And if you need to walk a bit through a water station, that's totally fine. Loads of people do it and still hit their time.
The bit I'm really struggling with isn't even the running. It's the rest of my life. My plan has me running at six in the morning three days a week and I'm just not a morning person.

What helped me was laying everything out the night before. Clothes on the chair, shoes by the door, watch charged. If I have to make a single decision at quarter to six, I'm crawling under the covers again.
That's genius. Remove all the decisions.
The problem is I'm also going to bed at like midnight.

Yeah, that's the real problem. Sleep is basically where the training actually happens. If you're on six hours a night with that mileage, you're going to get sick or hurt or just feel awful all the time.
So nine thirty bedtimes? I'll feel like a grandpa.

More like ten thirty, with your phone in another room. I know it sounds boring, but the difference in how your legs feel is massive. And before long runs, the night before the night before matters more than people think.
That's going to kill my Friday nights.
For four months. It's a season, it's not forever.
Tell that to my partner. Jess is already kind of annoyed. Sundays used to be our lazy brunch day, and now I disappear for two hours, come home, and fall asleep on the couch.
Oh, yeah. That's the hidden cost nobody puts in the plan.
She said the other day, you've become a person who talks about splits. And she's right.
You absolutely have. What if you made her part of it a little? Like she cycles alongside you for a bit of the long run, or meets you at the end and you do brunch after?
She'd probably like the brunch at the end part. Less so the cycling.

That still counts. Same with friends. I lost a bit of my social life training for my first one, but people started joining me on easy runs. You can't talk during intervals, but an easy run is basically a coffee date that moves.
Yeah, that's true. Honestly, talking through all this makes four months feel a lot less scary.
It's going to be hard, but you're in a better place than you think. Ten miles, a plan, and socks that aren't cotton.
The socks really are the breakthrough.
